content.targetText: A city replaced its first-come, first-served housing queue with a scoring system intended to favour applicants in greatest need. In the first report, officials celebrated a shorter average wait. The number was accurate, but the report did not say whose wait had shortened. Applicants with stable internet connections could correct an incomplete form within hours; those who relied on a public terminal often discovered an error only after the weekly ranking had closed. The council responded by adding an appeal period. That sounded like a remedy, although an appeal can restore a place only after someone has noticed that it was lost. An independent panel proposed publishing the scoring rules. Officials hesitated, fearing that applicants would tailor their answers. The panel replied that secrecy also lets an error masquerade as impartiality. Neither side could promise a system immune to strategic behaviour. The more revealing disagreement concerned what counted as evidence of need: a recent eviction notice, which is easy to verify, or years of precarious arrangements, which rarely produce a tidy document. Calling the first item "objective" may be administratively convenient; calling the second "subjective" quietly transfers the cost of proof to the person least able to pay it. The queue became faster. Whether it became fairer depends on whom the city has learned to see. A shorter average can coexist with much longer waits for a small group, especially when those applicants are repeatedly asked for evidence they cannot easily obtain. Publishing a single number therefore does more than simplify a report: it determines which experiences become legible as success and which disappear into the average.
